summary: Trinidad and Tobago lets citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada and most Commonwealth and Latin American countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days at the immigration officer's discretion, admits CARICOM nationals under Caribbean free movement for six months, and requires everyone else to obtain a visa from a Trinidad and Tobago mission before traveling.

passportValidity.text: Hold a passport valid for at least 6 months on arrival. Airlines apply this rule at check-in even where immigration would accept a passport that merely covers the length of stay.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis (ICVP)
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers aged 1 and over arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, including transits of more than 12 hours. Trinidad itself has forested areas where yellow fever circulates, so vaccination is also recommended for visitors going beyond the coastal towns, and it can be asked for by the next country you travel to.

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not required for entry and is not checked at the border. Public hospitals in Port of Spain and Scarborough handle emergencies but private care is billed up front, so coverage for treatment and repatriation is worth holding.

onwardTicket.text: Immigration officers expect visa-free visitors to show a return or onward ticket and the address where they will stay before deciding how many days to grant. Both are asked for on the immigration card.

proofOfFunds.text: No published minimum. Officers can ask visitors to demonstrate sufficient funds for the intended stay, and are more likely to do so for long stays or when no accommodation is booked.

declarations.name: Immigration Form and Customs Declaration
declarations.text: Every arriving passenger completes the paper immigration form (the ED card) and a customs declaration, handed out on board. The form asks for your address in Trinidad or Tobago and your departure date. The officer uses them to set the length of stay stamped in your passport.

currencyLimits.text: Currency and monetary instruments worth TTD 20,000 or more (or the foreign equivalent) must be declared to Customs on arrival and departure.

notes: Camouflage clothing and equipment are illegal for civilians in Trinidad and Tobago — items are confiscated at the airport and a fine is possible.
Firearms and ammunition require a permit issued in advance; penalties for undeclared weapons are severe.
Fresh produce, plants, meat and dairy are controlled by the plant and animal quarantine services. Declare them rather than risk a penalty.

payments.text: Cards work in supermarkets, malls, hotels and larger restaurants in Port of Spain, San Fernando and Crown Point, and ATMs are plentiful in town. Maxi-taxis, route taxis, doubles vendors, beach bars and rural shops are cash only. Keep small TT dollar notes on you.

safety.text: Trinidad has a high violent crime rate concentrated in specific areas of Port of Spain and the east-west corridor; several Western governments advise extra caution and the government has used states of emergency in recent years. Tourists are rarely targeted, but avoid walking at night, do not display valuables, and use pre-booked or hotel taxis rather than flagging cars. Tobago is markedly quieter, though break-ins to villas and rental cars occur.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Trinidad and Tobago Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: January to May is the dry season and covers Carnival, the country's defining event, in February or March. The wet season runs June to December; Trinidad and Tobago sit at the southern edge of the hurricane belt and are rarely hit directly, but heavy rain and flooding are common.

idp.text: Trinidad and Tobago is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Trinidad and Tobago yet.

tips.text: Carnival (the Monday and Tuesday before Ash Wednesday) fills every hotel room in Port of Spain months ahead and pushes prices up sharply. Book flights and accommodation half a year out, and expect immigration lines on arrival in Carnival week.

Stick to well-used areas after dark in Port of Spain, avoid Laventille, Beetham, Sea Lots and Morvant, and do not walk on unlit beaches at night in Tobago. Arrange transport in advance rather than hailing an unmarked car.

Trinidad and Tobago are one country but two very different trips — Trinidad is industrial, urban and where Carnival and the birdwatching are; Tobago is the beach and reef island. The domestic ferry and the 20-minute flight between them are both cheap, but ferry sailings sell out and are canceled in rough weather.

Leatherback turtles nest on Trinidad's north-east beaches, chiefly Matura and Grande Riviere, from March to August. Access is regulated. You need a permit or a licensed guide, arranged locally through the community groups that run the sites.

The officer decides how many days to grant on arrival and it is not always the full 90. Check the stamp before you leave the hall. To stay longer, apply for an extension of time to remain at the Immigration Division in Port of Spain well before the stamp expires.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Trinidad and Tobago?
faq.answer: Most visitors do not. Citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and most Commonwealth and Latin American countries enter visa-free, usually for up to 90 days. CARICOM nationals enter under Caribbean free movement with up to six months. Everyone else — including several Asian, Middle Eastern and African nationalities, and Venezuelan passport holders — must obtain a visa from a Trinidad and Tobago mission before traveling.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Trinidad and Tobago without a visa?
faq.answer: Up to 90 days, but the exact period is decided by the immigration officer and shorter stamps are common if your ticket shows a short trip. You can apply to the Immigration Division for an extension of time to remain before the stamp expires.

faq.question: What applies to CARICOM citizens?
faq.answer: Under the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas, CARICOM nationals arriving as visitors are entitled to a definite entry of up to six months provided they have no adverse immigration record and can support themselves. Skilled nationals with a CARICOM Skills Certificate can additionally live and work in the country.

faq.question: Can Venezuelan citizens travel to Trinidad and Tobago visa-free?
faq.answer: No. Trinidad and Tobago ended visa-free entry for Venezuelan nationals and a visa must now be obtained in advance. Given the small sea crossing between the two countries, immigration enforcement on this route is strict — do not travel on an informal boat and confirm current rules with the Immigration Division before booking.

faq.question: Do I need anything special to attend Carnival?
faq.answer: No separate permit or event visa exists — Carnival visitors enter on the normal visa-free stamp or visitor's visa. What you do need is early booking: accommodation, costumes with a mas band and fetes sell out months in advance, and flights into Piarco are at their most expensive that week.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination?
faq.answer: A certificate is required if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Beyond entry rules, vaccination is generally recommended for Trinidad itself because the virus circulates in its forests, and other countries may ask for a certificate when you arrive from Trinidad. Check before onward travel.
